questions.question: Describe the steps for sketching a tapered four-legged lattice tower in oblique projection on squared paper.
questions.expected_answer: Draw the front face feint as a tall trapezium, base line, two inward-sloping legs and a short top line, and tick the horizontal levels up the legs, closer together near the base. From the right-hand bottom and top corners draw depth lines back at 45 degrees along the grid diagonals, about half the real depth, and join their ends to form the back legs sloping like the front ones. Darken the visible legs, base and platform outlines, add horizontals on the two visible faces with the side ones receding at 45 degrees, draw a zigzag or X in each panel with single strokes, add a braced platform with antennas and a concrete base block, and annotate every part with labels, notes tied to the specifications, the height, the base size and the scale.

questions.question: Explain what makes two tower design ideas genuinely different and give an example pair.
questions.expected_answer: Ideas are different when they meet the brief by different structural routes rather than by different colours: a different number of legs, a different taper, a different bracing pattern such as zigzag, X or K, different member types such as card tubes, folded channels or straws, a different stability strategy such as a wide base, a weighted plate or outriggers, and a different way of softening the view. Example: a four-legged strongly tapered lattice with X bracing, card-tube legs and a wide base; and a three-legged slim tower with K bracing, folded channel legs, a weighted base plate and a card canopy hiding the antennas.

questions.question: List four sketching habits that earn design marks and explain why each matters.
questions.expected_answer: Feint construction lines first, checked against the brief, then dark outlines, with the construction lines left on the page: this gives correct proportions and shows the method. One clean stroke per member rather than many short ones: this keeps the sketch readable. Showing the bracing pattern fully in a few panels and noting that it continues: this avoids a grey tangle while still communicating the structure. Annotations that each answer a specification, with the height, base size and scale written on: this ties the drawing to the brief and shows design thinking rather than drawing skill alone.
